cases.title: Thirty Years’ War and the Westphalian settlement
cases.caution: The zones are approximate research extents, not surveyed borders. Confessional alignment, political control, and individual practice are separate variables.

sources.title: World History, Volume 2: The Protestant Reformation
sources.limitation: Case overview; it cannot resolve local boundaries or motives for every actor.

sources.title: Treaty of Westphalia
sources.limitation: Settlement text; it records legal provisions rather than population belief.

features.label: Holy Roman Empire before the war
features.summary: A politically fragmented imperial setting; the display does not collapse Imperial estates into one uniform state or confession.

features.label: Catholic, Lutheran, and Calvinist estates
features.summary: Multiple confessional establishments were present across the Empire. This qualitative zone is not a population-percentage map.

features.label: Major Central European conflict zone
features.summary: The conflict involved changing confessional, territorial, dynastic, and interstate coalitions.

features.label: Westphalian settlement
features.summary: The settlement addressed ecclesiastical liberty together with territorial, dynastic, and constitutional questions.

features.label: Post-settlement Imperial estates
features.summary: The settlement altered legal and territorial arrangements without proving immediate demographic or personal religious change.

states.label: Pre-conflict
states.summary: Fragmented political authority and multiple confessional establishments preceded the war.

states.label: Conflict
states.summary: A shifting war combined confessional alignments with territorial and geopolitical aims.

states.label: Immediate settlement
states.summary: Westphalian instruments addressed religion, territory, dynastic claims, and imperial arrangements.

states.label: Longer-term boundary
states.summary: Atlas records the settlement but lacks a reviewed local demographic layer for 1650; no population conversion is inferred.

deltas.summary: The settlement formalized ecclesiastical-liberty and territorial provisions within a wider constitutional settlement.
The retained sources do not support a precise local religion-by-population delta.

cases.title: Safavid state formation and Twelver Shiism
cases.caution: State policy, direct coercion, institutional sponsorship, scholarly movement, and later affiliation are shown separately. The map does not claim instant uniform conversion.

sources.title: World History, Volume 2: The Safavid Empire
sources.limitation: Broad synthesis; local timing and intensity varied.

sources.title: Sunni Survival in Safavid Iran
sources.limitation: Focused study of survival and persecution; not a complete demographic atlas.

features.label: Iran before Safavid state establishment
features.summary: Sunni communities and other religious traditions were present before the new state policy.

features.label: State proclamation at Tabriz
features.summary: Shah Ismail declared Twelver Shiism the state religion in 1501.

features.label: State-backed conversion pressure
features.summary: The cited overview documents conversion orders, exile, and lethal punishment for some resistance; intensity and chronology were not uniform.

features.label: Documented Sunni continuity
features.summary: Peer-reviewed scholarship documents Sunni survival and continued persecution beyond the initial proclamation.

features.label: State-supported Shia institutions
features.summary: State support for schools, shrines, and scholars contributed to a longer institutional transformation.

states.label: Pre-transition
states.summary: Religious presence before Safavid state establishment cannot be reduced to the later official identity.

states.label: State formation
states.summary: The new state declared an official religion and used direct pressure while building political authority.

states.label: Institutional expansion
states.summary: State sponsorship and coercive measures operated alongside surviving Sunni communities.

states.label: Longer-term outcome
states.summary: Iran underwent a long religious transformation; Atlas does not attribute every later affiliation solely to force.

deltas.summary: Twelver Shiism received official status and direct conversion pressure was documented.
Institutions expanded over time while Sunni survival contradicts an instant, complete transformation model.

flows.label: State sponsorship from the new Safavid center
flows.evidence: The state funded Shia schools and shrines and invited Shia scholars; this is an institutional mechanism, not a claim that every person converted along a route.
